messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Pham, a 52-year-old HVAC technician, had spent thirty years handling refrigerants without serious incident. That changed one humid August afternoon when he was working alone in the mechanical room of an apartment complex. A corroded valve on a chiller unit gave way without warning, releasing a pressurized cloud of R-22 gas directly into his face. The chemical hit his throat and lungs like a wall of ice and fire at the same time. He stumbled backward, coughing, gasping, unable to draw a full breath. By the time emergency responders arrived, he had collapsed on the concrete floor, his chest burning and his vision streaked with black spots. He spent three days in intensive care with chemical pneumonitis, and the doctors told him he was lucky—the exposure had been sublethal, but only just.

What Minh came to understand in the months that followed was that luck had nothing to do with safety. Back at work, he found himself unable to trust the equipment he had maintained for decades. He started checking and rechecking gauges, then moved on to checking the locks on his truck cab, then the deadbolts on his front door, then the windows. Even with his wife, Lan, sitting beside him in the living room, Minh could not convince himself that the air around him was safe. When she told him the house was fine, that the carbon monoxide detector was working, that no tank had sprung a leak, he heard her words but felt nothing—no shift, no relief. His body remained coiled, his shoulders up and his jaw tight, as though some invisible chemical agent were only seconds away from bursting into the space around him.

He began to avoid situations where his guard might drop. After work, he had always liked to sit on the back porch with a cup of tea and watch the birds. Now that felt impossible—relaxing felt like voluntarily putting down a shield, like waiting to be attacked. He stopped sitting anywhere without a clear path to the door. Lan would find him standing in the kitchen, eating his dinner over the counter, unwilling to settle into a chair. He avoided being alone in a room or a building altogether, following Lan from room to room, or keeping the television and radio on so the silence would not trick him into believing something was wrong. He also began to dodge anything that might involve stress: he turned down new jobs that required working with unfamiliar chemicals, stopped taking calls from anxious clients, and eventually asked his supervisor to assign him only the simplest residential tune-ups. The result was a steady drop in income; he took a pay cut and lost the respect of his younger colleagues, who whispered that he had lost his nerve.

The avoidance extended to his body itself. Minh was constantly scanning the inside of his own chest for tightness, for any sensation that might be the beginning of another chemical burn. He could not walk into a hardware store without checking the ceiling for compressed gas canisters, and several times he left a work site early because a faint smell reminded him of refrigerant. At home, he began checking the doors and windows three and four times before bed, often waking Lan with his movements. She tried to reassure him, but Minh’s reasoning had become fixed: if he allowed himself to feel safe, he would stop looking for danger, and the moment he stopped looking would be the moment danger returned.

What finally brought him to seek help was a panic attack in a big-box store. He had walked past a display of aerosol cans, and his chest seized, his vision tunneled, and a voice inside him said, *This is it, it’s happening again.* He ended up crouched between two shelves, gasping, until security escorted him outside. That evening, Lan told him she could not keep living this way—watching him suffer, watching him shrink his life. Minh agreed to see a clinician, though what he feared most was being told he would never feel safe again, and what he hoped for, in a quiet part of himself he barely acknowledged, was that someone might finally show him how to let the air back in.
